G5A01: At series resonance the inductive and capacitive reactances cancel, leaving only the circuit's resistance, so impedance falls to a minimum. Very high impedance at resonance describes a parallel LC circuit, not a series one.
G5A02: Reactance is the opposition that capacitors and inductors present to alternating current. Unlike resistance, it stores energy rather than dissipating it, and it changes with frequency.
G5A03: An inductor opposes AC through inductive reactance, XL = 2 pi f L. Reluctance sounds plausible but is opposition to magnetic flux in a magnetic circuit, not to current.
G5A04: A capacitor opposes AC through capacitive reactance, XC = 1/(2 pi f C). Conductance and admittance measure how easily current flows, the opposite idea.
G5A05: Inductive reactance is XL = 2 pi f L, so it rises in direct proportion to frequency. The amplitude of the AC has no effect on reactance.
G5A06: Capacitive reactance is XC = 1/(2 pi f C), so it falls as frequency rises. Amplitude does not change reactance.
G5A07: Admittance (Y) is the reciprocal of impedance, Y = 1/Z, measured in siemens. Conductance is only the inverse of resistance, and susceptance only the inverse of reactance.
G5A08: Impedance is the ratio of voltage to current, Z = E/I, Ohm's law extended to AC circuits. The ratio of current to voltage is admittance, its inverse.
G5A09: Reactance is opposition to current, so like resistance and impedance it is measured in ohms. The siemens is the unit for the inverses: conductance, susceptance and admittance.
G5A10: All listed items are true: a transformer, a Pi-network and a suitable length of transmission line (such as a quarter-wave section) can each transform one impedance to another at RF.
G5A11: Reactance uses the symbol X, as in XL and XC. Z is impedance, B is susceptance and Y is admittance.
G5A12: At resonance XL equals XC, and because they are opposite in phase they cancel, leaving only resistance. Resistance itself is not cancelled.
G5B01: A doubling or halving of power is 10 log(2) = about 3 dB. 6 dB is a factor of four in power, or of two in voltage.
G5B02: In a parallel circuit every branch has the same voltage, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents (Kirchhoff's current law). Adding branches increases total current, not decreases it.
G5B03: P = E squared / R = 400 x 400 / 800 = 200 watts.
G5B04: P = E x I = 12 V x 0.2 A = 2.4 watts.
G5B05: P = I squared x R = (0.007 A) squared x 1,250 ohms = 0.06125 W, about 61 milliwatts.
G5B06: 200 V peak-to-peak is 100 V peak, and 100 x 0.707 = 70.7 V RMS. PEP = E squared / R = 70.7 x 70.7 / 50 = 100 watts.
G5B07: The RMS (root mean square) value of an AC signal is defined as the DC voltage that would heat a resistor equally. Peak and peak-to-peak values are larger than the effective value.
G5B08: Peak = 120 x 1.414 = 169.7 V, and peak-to-peak is twice that: 2 x 169.7 = 339.4 volts. 169.7 V is only the peak value.
G5B09: RMS = peak x 0.707 = 17 x 0.707 = about 12 volts.
G5B10: A 1 dB loss leaves 10^(-0.1) = 0.794 of the power, so the loss is 1 - 0.794 = 0.206, about 20.6 percent.
G5B11: An unmodulated carrier has a constant envelope, so its peak envelope power equals its average power, a ratio of 1.00.
G5B12: E = square root of (P x R) = square root of (1200 x 50) = square root of 60,000 = about 245 volts RMS.
G5B13: An unmodulated carrier's envelope never varies, so PEP equals average power: 1060 watts.
G5B14: 500 V peak-to-peak is 250 V peak, and 250 x 0.707 = 176.8 V RMS. PEP = 176.8 x 176.8 / 50 = about 625 watts.
G5C01: The changing magnetic field from the primary current links the secondary winding and induces a voltage in it. This coupling between two coils is mutual inductance.
G5C02: A transformer works in both directions. Feeding a 4:1 step-down transformer from its secondary makes it a 1:4 step-up transformer, so the input voltage is multiplied by 4.
G5C03: 1/R = 1/10 + 1/20 + 1/50 = 0.1 + 0.05 + 0.02 = 0.17, so R = 1/0.17 = about 5.9 ohms. Parallel resistance is always less than the smallest resistor.
G5C05: Power in equals power out, so the side with lower voltage carries more current. In a step-up transformer that is the primary, which needs heavier wire.
G5C06: Output voltage scales with the turns ratio: 120 V x (1500 / 500) = 120 x 3 = 360 volts.
G5C07: Turns ratio = square root of the impedance ratio = square root of (600 / 50) = square root of 12 = about 3.5 to 1. 12 to 1 is the impedance ratio, not the turns ratio.
G5C08: Parallel capacitances add: 5.0 nF + 5.0 nF + 0.75 nF (750 pF) = 10.75 nanofarads.
G5C09: Equal capacitors in series give the value of one divided by how many there are: 100 microfarads / 3 = 33.3 microfarads.
G5C10: Equal inductors in parallel give the value of one divided by how many there are: 10 mH / 3 = 3.3 millihenries.
G5C11: Series inductances add like series resistors: 20 mH + 50 mH = 70 millihenries.
G5C12: Series capacitors combine like parallel resistors: C = (20 x 50) / (20 + 50) = 1000 / 70 = about 14.3 microfarads.
G5C13: Capacitances in parallel add, so a capacitor in parallel raises the total. A capacitor in series lowers the total capacitance.
G5C14: Inductances in series add, so an inductor in series raises the total. An inductor in parallel lowers it.
G6A01: Discharging a 12-volt lead-acid battery below about 10.5 volts damages the plates and shortens its life. Going down to 8.5 or 6 volts would be a deep discharge that harms the battery.
G6A02: Low internal resistance means little voltage is lost inside the battery under load, so it can deliver high current. That suits loads like transceivers on transmit.
G6A03: A germanium diode begins to conduct at about 0.3 volts forward bias, lower than the roughly 0.7 volts of a silicon diode.
G6A04: Electrolytic capacitors pack a large capacitance into a small volume, which is why they are used as power supply filters. They have loose tolerances and relatively high leakage.
G6A05: A silicon junction diode starts to conduct at about 0.7 volts forward bias. About 0.3 volts is the figure for germanium.
G6A06: A wire-wound resistor is a coil of wire, so it has inductance. At RF that inductance adds reactance and makes circuit behavior unpredictable.
G6A07: A transistor switch is driven either fully on (saturation) or fully off (cutoff). The active region in between is used for linear amplification.
G6A08: Low voltage ceramic capacitors are cheap and widely used for bypassing. Their tolerance and stability are generally not as good as other types.
G6A09: In a MOSFET the gate is a metal (or polysilicon) electrode insulated from the channel by a thin oxide layer, which gives it a very high input impedance. A back-biased junction gate describes a JFET.
G6A10: The control grid, between cathode and plate, sets how many electrons reach the plate; a small voltage on it controls a large plate current. The screen and suppressor grids serve other purposes.
G6A11: Above its self-resonant frequency, the capacitance between an inductor's turns dominates, so the component acts like a capacitor rather than an inductor.
G6A12: The screen grid sits between the control grid and the plate and shields them from each other, reducing grid-to-plate capacitance. That helps prevent unwanted oscillation.
G6B01: A ferrite core's behavior at different frequencies depends on its composition, called the mix. Different mixes are chosen for different frequency ranges.
G6B02: MMIC stands for Monolithic Microwave Integrated Circuit, a small IC amplifier or other block made for VHF, UHF and microwave work.
G6B03: CMOS logic draws very little current except when switching, so it uses far less power than TTL.
G6B04: A 50-ohm BNC connector keeps a low SWR up to about 4 GHz. Above that its performance falls off.
G6B05: All listed items are true: a ferrite toroid gives large inductance with few turns, its core mix can be chosen for a frequency range, and its closed shape keeps most of the magnetic field inside the core.
G6B06: An op-amp is an analog device: it amplifies continuously varying signals rather than handling digital on/off levels.
G6B07: The type N connector is a threaded, weather-resistant RF connector that works well up to about 10 GHz, making it popular for VHF, UHF and microwave feed lines.
G6B08: An LED emits light when it is forward biased and current flows through the junction. Reverse biased, it does not conduct and gives no light.
G6B10: A ferrite bead or core around the coax adds impedance to current flowing on the outside of the shield, which reduces that common-mode current. It does not convert or cancel the current.
G6B11: SMA (SubMiniature version A) is a small threaded coaxial connector that works to several gigahertz, common on handheld radios and microwave gear.
G6B12: RCA phono connectors are cheap and common for audio, low frequency and DC connections such as accessory jacks. PL-259, BNC and type N are RF connectors.
G7A01: A bleeder resistor across the filter capacitors drains their stored charge after power is removed, so the supply is safe to work on. It is not a fuse.
G7A02: Capacitors and inductors smooth the pulsating DC from the rectifier: capacitors hold up the voltage and inductors oppose changes in current. Diodes rectify, they do not filter.
G7A03: A full-wave center-tap rectifier uses two diodes, each conducting on alternate half cycles from opposite ends of a center-tapped winding. A full-wave bridge uses four diodes and needs no center tap.
G7A04: A half-wave rectifier needs only one diode. Its ripple frequency equals the AC frequency, half that of a full-wave rectifier.
G7A05: A half-wave rectifier conducts only on one half of each cycle, so 180 degrees of the 360-degree cycle is converted to DC.
G7A06: A full-wave rectifier uses both halves of the cycle, so all 360 degrees is converted to DC.
G7A07: A full-wave rectifier turns each half cycle into a positive pulse, so the output is DC pulses at twice the input frequency (120 pulses a second from 60 Hz).
G7A08: A switchmode supply runs at high frequency, so its transformers and filter components can be much smaller and lighter than those of a linear supply.
G7B01: Neutralizing feeds back a signal that cancels the unwanted feedback through the amplifying device's internal capacitance, which eliminates self-oscillation.
G7B02: A Class C amplifier conducts for less than half the cycle, so it wastes the least power and is the most efficient, though it is not linear.
G7B03: A two-input AND gate gives a high output only when both inputs are high; any low input makes the output low.
G7B04: A Class A amplifier conducts for the whole cycle, 100 percent of the time, which makes it very linear but inefficient.
G7B05: A 3-bit counter has 2 x 2 x 2 = 2^3 = 8 states, counting 0 through 7.
G7B06: A shift register is a clocked chain of flip-flops; on each clock pulse the stored data moves one step along the chain.
G7B07: A sine wave oscillator needs an amplifier and a frequency-selective filter, with the filter's output fed back to the amplifier's input in phase to sustain oscillation.
G7B08: Efficiency = RF output power / DC input power. For example, 600 W out from 1000 W of DC input is 60 percent efficient.
G7B09: An LC oscillator runs at the resonant frequency of its tank circuit, f = 1/(2 pi times the square root of LC), so the inductance and capacitance set the frequency.
G7B10: A linear amplifier produces an output that is a faithful, larger copy of its input waveform, which is needed for modes like SSB. Class C is not linear.
G7B11: FM carries information only in frequency, with constant amplitude, so a nonlinear Class C stage can amplify it without distortion. SSB and AM need a linear amplifier.
G7C01: A balanced modulator produces both sidebands with the carrier suppressed; a sharp filter then passes one sideband and rejects the other to make SSB.
G7C02: A balanced modulator cancels the carrier and outputs both sidebands, called double-sideband suppressed-carrier RF.
G7C03: A matching transformer converts the feed line or load impedance to the impedance the transmitter is designed for, so power transfers efficiently.
G7C04: A product detector mixes the incoming SSB (or CW) signal with a locally generated carrier to recover the audio in a single sideband receiver.
G7C05: A DDS creates its output digitally from a crystal-controlled clock, so its frequency can be changed in fine steps while keeping crystal stability. Its output is not perfectly pure.
G7C06: DSP filters are defined in software, so a wide range of bandwidths and shapes can be created and changed easily, which is hard with fixed analog components.
G7C07: Insertion loss is how much a filter attenuates signals inside its passband. Ultimate rejection is how well it blocks signals outside the passband.
G7C08: All listed items are true: input amplifier gain, demodulator bandwidth and input amplifier noise figure all affect how weak a signal a receiver can detect.
G7C09: The I (in-phase) and Q (quadrature) signals are 90 degrees apart, which lets an SDR represent both amplitude and phase of a signal.
G7C10: With I and Q signals, software can produce any combination of amplitude and phase, so all types of modulation can be created with the right processing.
G7C11: All listed items are true: in an SDR, filtering, detection and modulation are done by software operating on the digitized signal.
G7C12: The cutoff frequency is where output power falls to half the input, the 3 dB point; above it a low-pass filter attenuates more.
G7C13: Ultimate rejection is the most attenuation a filter can give signals well outside its passband. Insertion loss is the loss inside the passband.
G7C14: A band-pass filter's bandwidth is measured between its upper and lower half-power (3 dB down) frequencies.
